finding: There is no live range for a one-coil job yet (the site's existing $100-$700 range is for the coil job in general and is checked in the full-set file). Built totals for ONE coil (one coil + the stated hours x $120-$160 per hour, the national middle rate used for this arithmetic): economy 2015 Mazda3 2.0L $125-$274; midsize 2024 Ford Explorer 2.3L $154-$231; truck 2024 Ford Ranger 2.3L $178-$231; luxury 2024 Lincoln Corsair 2.0L $112-$154. Across the four that is roughly $110-$275 before diagnosis, for a four-cylinder. That now overlaps the outside estimates instead of sitting under them: Jerry $142-$234 for one coil, RepairPal $238-$320 (number of coils not stated), J.D. Power $100-$300 for a single conventional coil and $200-$600 per coil on coil-on-plug engines. It is still at the lower end, because six of the eight labor figures are manufacturer warranty times (the low end of what shops bill) and no diagnosis fee is included. It should not be read as covering six- and eight-cylinder or European luxury engines. What changed on the second attempt. Parts: the Mazda3 low is now an NGK coil at $88.78 on a page that prints 'Condition:New' and names the Mazda 3 2.0L SkyActiv engine and Mazda number PE20-18-100 (the page prints no model years); the $44.95 coil on a page with no condition is kept only as a cross-check. The Explorer low is now the Motorcraft DG576 coil at $106.25 (new, sold each, page names the 20-24 Explorer 2.3L) instead of the $16.37 discount price of the $26.00 genuine coil, because that cheap coil has no second independent price and the catalog does not say which 2024 builds take it. The Lincoln Corsair still rests on the $26.00 genuine coil (P2GZ-12029-A, $16.37 at a discount seller stating New condition): no Denso, NGK, Delphi, Bosch, Motorcraft-boxed or Standard coil for the 2023-2025 Corsair 2.0L was found on a page stating new, only a Walker coil at $16.23 on a page with no condition, so that class is unchanged and remains the cheapest job here. Labor: the low in every class is still the manufacturer time for the example vehicle (Mazda 0.3 hour; Ford 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 hour). For the Mazda3 and the Explorer the high is now 0.6 hour, taken from a general guide that gives 0.3-0.6 hours for one coil-on-plug coil on a four-cylinder or inline-six; the page names no author and is not vehicle-specific, so it is the weakest labor source here, and if it is not accepted those two classes fall back to $125-$226 and $154-$199. How solid the manufacturer times are: none is a bare 'replace one coil' line. Ford TSB 26-2210 words its one-coil operations 'Retrieve DTCs; Inspect Date Code On Related Ignition Coil(s); Replace One Ignition Coil': 0.4 Hrs on the 2024-2025 Explorer 2.3L, 0.6 Hrs on the 2024 Ranger 2.3L and 0.8 Hrs on the 2024-2025 Escape/Corsair 2.0L, which includes reading the stored codes and the date code on top of the coil. The same bulletin gives one-coil times of 0.3 to 0.5 Hrs for the Maverick 2.0L, Mustang 2.3L, Bronco 2.3L, Bronco Sport and Escape 1.5L. Mazda TSB 01-014/16 allows a single 0.3 hour for swap-testing and replacing anywhere from one to four coils on the 2014-16 Mazda3. Six-cylinder and luxury evidence found, all cross-checks and none used for a range: GM bulletin PIP5038B gives the 2008-2009 Cadillac CTS and STS 3.6L V6 '.2 hr' for 'Spark Plug and Ignition Coil Replacement' on one cylinder (it covers the plug as well, plus .1 hr for each additional cylinder and up to .5 hr diagnosis), and '.7 hr' for the bank under the intake on the transverse Enclave/Traverse/Acadia/Outlook; the genuine CTS coil 12632479 lists at $121.60 and a Delphi coil sells for $51.99 on a page with no condition. On those figures a one-coil job on that Cadillac would build to roughly the same money as the four-cylinders here, but the time is not a pure coil time so it is not used. GM bulletin PIP6073 gives the 2025 Escalade '.5' with no unit for swap-testing and replacing one coil. BMW bulletin SI B12 18 14 has an operation 'Replacing one ignition coil' but prints no time. Where the rear coils sit under the intake, stated times are much longer: a parts maker (BWD) says coil replacement 'can take between 2-4 hours' on such engines and lists Cadillac ATS, CTS, SRX, STS, XTS and Lexus RX350 among them; a general guide gives 1.5-2.5 hours for rear coils on a transverse V6; trade press quotes Nissan at 2.2 hours for all six coils on a 2004-and-newer Maxima. None of those is a one-coil time for a named luxury car, and the GM and BWD statements about the CTS V6 do not agree with each other, so no six-cylinder or European luxury class was built. Still missing: a manufacturer-stated one-coil time with a unit for a six-cylinder or European luxury car together with a genuine list price and a new aftermarket price for it; a second, mainstream-brand new price for the Corsair coil; a model-year line for the Mazda3 on the NGK page. Caveats on parts carried over: the Mazda dealer catalog page shows $178.32 and $133.71 without labelling them, the Ranger catalog page likewise shows two unlabelled prices, and dealer-catalog prices are per coil without the word 'each'. Confidence is kept low while the file is held: two of the eight labor figures are from a general guide, the manufacturer times include a code read or swap test, and the luxury example is a four-cylinder with an unusually cheap coil. Not covered: engines where the intake manifold must come off to reach the rear coils (many transverse V6s), six- and eight-cylinder engines, and older engines with a single coil pack and plug wires.
extras: A quote usually adds a diagnosis fee, because the shop first has to confirm which coil has failed; that is not in these figures. Many shops bill a minimum labor charge of half an hour or an hour even for a quick job. The spark plug in the same cylinder is often replaced at the same time, and the coil boot if it is cracked or oil-soaked. A valve cover gasket may be added if oil is found in the plug well. On a high-mileage engine shops often recommend replacing all the coils when one fails, which multiplies the parts cost by the number of cylinders. Shop supplies and sales tax are extra. A misfire that has been driven on for a long time can damage the catalytic converter, which is a separate and much larger repair.
